reviewType: Second AI-assisted editorial review; not independent human certification
scope: Conceptual validity of a substantive sample of discussion links and all ten substantive Nihāya no-direct-route classifications. Not a fresh source collation or exhaustive certification of every network edge.
method: Read the 22 paired canonical English discussions and relevant surrounding paragraphs; checked Arabic passages where conceptual wording or scope required it.
Read all ten substantive nonparallel Nihāya English bodies in full and inspected the specified candidate Bidāya or Muzaffar counterparts.
Assess argumentative relationship, distinctions, author-versus-reported-view attribution, and necessary cautions. Exact quotes establish the reviewed locations rather than replacing semantic review.

Capture current complete file hashes, unit Arabic/English body hashes, and matched-paragraph hashes. These bind the reviewed sources but do not imply that every paragraph of every referenced source unit underwent a new full collation.

substantiveNonparallelCases.reason: The advanced chapter contains direct counterparts for the logical distinction between necessary and coincidental conditionals, and the primary/common-predication resolution of the absolute-nonexistence paradox. Its full analysis is more extensive, but the navigation standard is discussion-level.

Its opening graded-potentiality argument repeats the sperm/food example and inference from positive proximity and intensity. Bidāya also supplies related continuous-form foundations; the precise proposed route uses the opening argument.

This unit specifically changes the relata of origination from quiddity and cause to two existences under existential primacy. The inspected Bidāya account names temporal, intrinsic, and dahri origination, without a distinct exposition of this additional division. Shared causal-dependence foundations remain possible.

The active/passive/neither classification and the quoted Asfar synthesis of graded knowledge have no matching introductory division in the inspected counterparts. Bidāya XI.10 paragraph 4 overlaps its union doctrine, so this is not a claim that the unit has no shared foundations.

The earlier exclusion considered the divine-unity chapter but overlooked Bidāya XII.3, whose proof from the bestowal of beings, effects, and relations explicitly concludes sole lordship. Nihāya supplies further order and cooperation arguments.

The essential/active division of decree and the restriction of measure to material attributes and effects have no distinct counterpart in the inspected Bidāya chapter. Bidāya XII.5 paragraph 16 reports Peripatetic providential knowledge, then criticizes its acquired-form model. It must not be equated without qualification with Nihāya XII.12 paragraph 2, which identifies providential knowledge with the divine essence.

The earlier exclusion overlooked Bidāya XII.9’s explicit three-realm causal hierarchy and correspondence with divine knowledge. Nihāya uses this shared structure to infer the best possible order; the link must distinguish the premise from the stronger conclusion.

The prior reason referred only to brief material impediments. Bidāya XII.3 in fact contains the same privation example and fivefold good/evil classification. The pain objection and explicit divine-decree treatment remain later developments.

Bidāya’s general origination definitions and its account of cosmic flux provide background, but the inspected passages do not reproduce Nihāya’s complete proof of whole-world origination and its extended critique of a prior empty time. This is a scoped selection decision, not denial of every possible foundation link.

The derivation of uninterrupted emanation, rejection of cosmic cycles, and warning about unknown conditions in allegedly complete causes are distinctive in the inspected material. General dependence and renewal passages are not identical to this conclusion.
